title: Zoho's Sridhar Vembu Wants India to Shut Down Its Business Schools
excerpt: Endorsing a Cambridge professor's New York Times essay, the Zoho co-founder says India should shift from MBA schools to startup incubators and venture creation.
body:
• Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu has called for shutting down business schools in India, saying the focus should shift to startup incubators, venture creation and experimentation.
  • Vembu was reacting to a New York Times opinion piece by Cambridge professor Chris Marquis, who argued business schools have strayed from developing responsible leaders toward steering students to lucrative careers.
  • Marquis's wider case, as reported, is that MBA programmes mint profit-focused managers — and he proposed multidisciplinary programmes in their place; other academics have pushed back.
  • No policy change is proposed by any government in the reporting — this is a debate about what an MBA is for, not a closure plan.

One of India's best-known software founders wants the MBA gone. Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu has called for shutting down business schools in India and shifting the focus to startup incubators, venture creation and experimentation, according to reporting of his remarks. Vembu said he has been making the argument for two decades, the reporting added.

The essay Vembu was endorsing

Vembu was reacting to a New York Times opinion piece by Chris Marquis, a professor at the University of Cambridge who has also taught at Harvard and Cornell. Marquis argued that business schools have strayed from developing responsible leaders, instead steering students toward lucrative careers.

https://x.com/sunilgurjar01/status/2116817533965676678

As Morning Brew summarised the essay, Marquis claims that unlike law or medical schools, which teach students to maximise social good, MBA programmes prioritise minting high-paid managers singularly focused on profit. He cited research from Nobel-winning economist Daron Acemoglu suggesting that firms run by MBAs tend to redistribute profits from workers to shareholders while not growing faster, and he criticised business-school case studies for oversimplifying reality and omitting negative facts about companies. His proposed replacement was not nothing: multidisciplinary business programmes examining issues through a broader lens, incorporating "questions of history, democracy and ecological limits."

"Questions of history, democracy and ecological limits."

— Chris Marquis's proposed replacement for MBA programmes, as summarised by Morning Brew

The pushback

The argument has not gone unanswered. Copenhagen Business School professor Nicolai J. Foss seconded many of Marquis's criticisms but argued it might not be realistic to teach managers to prioritise social benefit, which is difficult to define and measure, and questioned the implication that profit-seeking is divorced from producing societal value. Morning Brew also noted that the financial return on many MBA programmes — tuition against the pay bump graduates can expect — has declined over the past year, per Bloomberg's calculations.

What Vembu would put in its place

Vembu's version of the replacement, as reported, is practical rather than academic: startup incubators, venture creation and experimentation in place of business schools in India. That is a founder's answer from a company-builder — and it is a proposal in a debate, not a policy. No government programme in the reporting adopts it, and no Indian institution has announced any such closure.

For Indian students and diaspora families weighing an MBA, the immediate takeaway is narrower: a prominent employer is publicly questioning what the degree certifies. Whether business schools answer by reforming — the route other academics in the debate favour — or the argument fades as a provocation is the part to watch.
nri_angle: A leading Indian founder publicly questioning the MBA matters to diaspora families weighing expensive business degrees for their children.
author: Diaspora Desk
